summary: Discourages introducing software defects, in general and in network protocol implementations specifically. It notes that defects are among the largest cost drivers in networking and clarifies best current practice. It is informational and widely understood as a lighthearted piece.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 9225 is an April 1st document about the harms caused by software defects. It uses serious-sounding requirements and deliberately absurd recommendations to make its point.

subtitle: An April 1st RFC states the obvious: software defects cause harm.

tldr.problem: Software defects can cause system failures and financial costs, including in network protocol implementations.
tldr.mechanism: This April 1st RFC uses deadpan requirements and examples to discourage introducing defects and to suggest documenting them when they occur.
tldr.outcome: Its advice mixes serious concerns about defects with deliberately absurd guidance, making it a humorous reminder rather than a technical defect-removal procedure.

today: RFC 9225 is an Informational document published on April 1, 2022. It is a humorous statement about the harms software defects can cause.

sections.title: The Case Against Software Defects
sections.content: RFC 9225 defines software defects, informally called bugs, as errors, flaws, or faults that cause incorrect or unexpected results. Its central requirement says implementers must not introduce bugs. The document is dated April 1 and delivers this obvious advice in a dry, formal style.
sections.plainLanguage: A bug is a mistake that makes a program produce an incorrect or unexpected result. This April 1st RFC says not to introduce bugs, as if that needed a formal rule.

sections.title: Examples of High-Impact Defects
sections.content: The RFC describes software failures involving the Ariane 5 launch, the Deep Impact spacecraft, and a Soviet early-warning satellite. It also cites a study estimating that programming bugs cost about 0.6 percent of gross domestic product. The examples show how software defects can affect systems and people.
sections.plainLanguage: The document points to failures involving a rocket, a spacecraft, and an early-warning satellite. It uses them to show that software defects can have serious consequences.

sections.title: The Document's Best Practices
sections.content: The RFC lists six practices, including not implementing bugs, clearly documenting bugs that are introduced, and assuming that external and internal input may result from bugs. It also jokes that broken specifications should be implemented by combining smaller bugs into a larger one and that “It's not a bug, it's a feature” is rude.
sections.plainLanguage: The document says to avoid defects and document them when they occur. Its advice about combining bugs and the “feature” excuse is deliberately humorous.
